1394.title: Mass intentions
1394.hook: a Mass can be offered for someone living or dead; any offering is a gift, not a price
1394.howItsDone: Catholics ask a parish to have a Mass offered for a living or deceased person, usually through the parish office, and the intention is often listed in the bulletin or mentioned at that Mass. Some give an offering when they ask; Church law forbids any appearance of buying the Mass and urges priests to accept intentions from the poor without one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, requiem: the old prayer of rest and light for the dead. Your line was let perpetual light shine.

The back page of a parish bulletin, under the Mass times. Saturday evening: for Maria Lopez, deceased. Sunday morning: for the Kowalski family. Tuesday: in thanksgiving, for a safe surgery. Wednesday: for a grandmother, on her birthday. On Saturday evening the priest says it aloud, near the start or in the prayers: this Mass is offered for Maria. A few people in the pews look up. One of them is the one who asked. What does it mean to say a Mass is for someone? And what about the envelope that went to the parish office?
screen: `THE BACK PAGE OF THE BULLETIN.` → `THIS MASS IS OFFERED FOR MARIA.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE ENVELOPE?`

segments.voice: Start with an old root. In the second book of Maccabees, after a battle, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection and sends the silver to Jerusalem so a sacrifice can be offered for the soldiers who died. That's the passage that closed with yesterday's holy and wholesome thought. Catholics see in it the shape of a Mass intention: an offering, a sacrifice, and a particular person held up to God. Who can a Mass be for? Anyone: a sick friend, a newborn, a marriage on its anniversary, a soldier far away. Church law says a priest is free to apply the Mass for anyone, living or dead. It doesn't have to be a Catholic. Then the envelope. Church law allows a priest to accept an offering from someone who asks for a Mass for their intention, but insists there must be no hint of trade or commerce in it. The offering is a gift that supports the Church and its priests, not a price that buys a Mass. The law even urges priests to celebrate Mass for the intentions of the faithful, especially the poor, without receiving any offering at all. If you can't give, you can still ask. Last, what an intention does. Saturday's Mass isn't a different Mass, and Maria isn't the only person it touches. The whole Church prays, and Christ's offering is the same. The intention names one face inside it, like holding up one photograph in a crowded room and saying, especially her.

segments.voice: Ask who comes to mind first: someone who has died, someone sick, someone starting something new, someone you worry about and can't help. Let one person settle, hold their face, and wish them every good thing for one long breath. If you're Catholic, or would like to be part of this, you might plan to call a parish office and ask for a Mass for them; if not, keep them close.

1395.title: The Eucharistic fast
1395.hook: one hour without food before communion
1395.howItsDone: Catholics in the Latin Church abstain from food and drink, except water and medicine, for at least one hour before receiving communion. The elderly, the sick and those caring for them are excused.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mass intentions: one name held up inside the whole Mass, and an offering that's a gift, not a price. Your line was a mass for them.

Sunday, a quarter past nine. Mass is at ten. In the kitchen, someone reaches for a granola bar, stops, glances at the clock on the stove, and does a bit of arithmetic. Communion comes partway through, so is there time? Coffee, yes or no? A glass of water is fine, isn't it? It's a small, slightly comic moment, repeated in Catholic kitchens on Sunday mornings: grown adults doing math about a granola bar. But under the math is something serious. Why would the Church ask anyone to go a little hungry before receiving bread?
screen: `A GRANOLA BAR AND A CLOCK.` → `MATH IN THE KITCHEN.` → `WHY GO A LITTLE HUNGRY?`

segments.voice: First, the rule, from the Church's law: someone who is going to receive the Eucharist abstains from all food and drink for at least one hour before communion. Before communion, not before Mass, so the clock runs to the moment you receive, not to the opening hymn. Second, what's allowed. The same law sets aside water and medicine; neither breaks the fast. And it adds something gentle: the elderly, the sick and the people who care for them may receive communion even if they've eaten within the hour. The rule bends toward the people who need it to bend. Third, why. Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger." The fast lets the body take part in that sentence. A little emptiness makes the bread stand out. It marks this food as different from breakfast, and gives a short stretch, in the car, in the pew, to want what you're about to receive. Last, how small it is. One hour isn't heroic, and that's partly the point: it's a fast sized for families with toddlers, for shift workers, for anyone. Because it's small, it's easy to forget, which is why the granola-bar arithmetic happens at all. And the question under the arithmetic is a good one. Am I coming to this hungry? Or full, and distracted, and not really expecting anything?

segments.voice: Notice your body: is there any hunger in it, or thirst? Don't fix it; just notice where it sits, then ask what you're hungry for underneath the food: rest, company, forgiveness, quiet, a sense that things will be all right. If you pray, offer that hunger to God; if you don't, stay with it, kindly, a little longer.

1396.title: Lenten customs
1396.hook: Friday fish, Stations, and a box for the poor
1396.howItsDone: In Lent, Catholics abstain from meat on Fridays, and some parishes hold fish fries and pray the Stations of the Cross on Friday evenings. Some families keep a box or jar for alms at home and give what they save to the poor at the end of Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharistic fast: an hour of going without before communion. Your line was hungry for him.

A Friday in March. The church hall smells of fried fish, and a volunteer in an apron is handing out paper plates of cod and coleslaw. Upstairs, at seven, a small group walks slowly around the church, stopping at each of the stations on the walls. At home, on the kitchen counter, sits a little cardboard box with a slot in the top, and the coins rattle when someone moves it to wipe the counter. None of this happens at Mass. It happens in halls, hallways and kitchens, where Lent lives as much as in church.
screen: `FISH IN THE CHURCH HALL.` → `STATIONS AT SEVEN.` → `A BOX ON THE KITCHEN COUNTER.`

segments.voice: You met these three in your first year: prayer, fasting and almsgiving. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says to do all three quietly. On alms, the Douay-Rheims has him say: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Each custom fits under one of them. Friday fish belongs to fasting. Church law makes Fridays days of penance and names abstinence from meat as a Friday practice, kept with special care in Lent. Fish isn't counted as meat, so it often lands on the Friday table, and some parishes hold fish fries. The point isn't the fish. It's the meat you went without, and the reminder that Friday is the day of the cross. The Stations of the Cross belong to prayer. On Lenten Fridays, some parishes walk the stations together, stopping at each image of Jesus's last journey, from his condemnation to the tomb. It's a prayer you do with your feet. The box for the poor belongs to almsgiving. Families keep a small box or jar through Lent, drop in what they saved by skipping a treat or eating simply, and bring it to church at the end. That's the quiet logic of Lent: the three feed each other. What you give up in fasting, you give away in alms, and you carry both into prayer. It works best in a kitchen, on an ordinary weekday, with nobody watching. Left hand, right hand.

segments.voice: Look at the three: going without something, like meat on a Friday; walking and praying, like the Stations; setting money aside for someone in need, like the box on the counter. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, decide quietly and tell no one.

1397.title: Advent customs
1397.hook: a tree of ornaments telling the story from creation to Christ
1397.howItsDone: Some Catholic families, schools and parishes keep a Jesse tree in Advent: a branch or small tree on which an ornament is hung each day, each standing for a figure or story from the Bible, with a short reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lenten customs: fish in the hall, the Stations at seven, a box on the counter. Your line was lent at home.

Early December. A bare branch stands in a pot of stones on the dining table. No lights, no tinsel. Each evening after dinner, a child is allowed to hang one homemade ornament on it, and someone reads a short passage from the Bible. A paper apple. A tiny wooden boat. A ram cut out of felt. A ladder made of popsicle sticks. A coat with too many colors. By Christmas the branch is crowded, and anyone who sat at that table has heard a whole story, a few minutes a night, from the garden to the manger.
screen: `A BARE BRANCH IN A POT OF STONES.` → `ONE ORNAMENT A NIGHT.` → `FROM THE GARDEN TO THE MANGER.`

segments.voice: The name comes from Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root." An old root, and out of it, something new and green. Christians read that shoot as the Messiah, growing from the family line of David. So who's Jesse? Not a king. In the first book of Samuel he's a man of Bethlehem with a house full of sons, and his youngest is out minding the sheep when the prophet comes looking for a king. That youngest boy is David. So the prophecy reaches back behind the king, to an ordinary household in Bethlehem. Matthew's Gospel names him in the long genealogy at its very start: "And Obed begot Jesse. And Jesse begot David the king." Then, the ornaments. Each one stands for a person or a moment in that family story. A piece of fruit, for Adam and Eve; Genesis never says it was an apple. A boat, for Noah. A ram, for Abraham and Isaac. A ladder, for Jacob's dream. A coat, for Joseph. Families choose their own sets, so no two Jesse trees look quite the same. Last, why Advent, the season of waiting you met in your first year. The Jesse tree shows what the waiting was made of: generations of people, some flawed, some surprising, gathered on one branch as the story that leads to Jesus, read aloud one name at a time.

1398.title: Twelve days
1398.hook: Christmas runs from the 25th to Epiphany and beyond
1398.howItsDone: Catholics keep Christmas as a season, from Christmas Day through the Epiphany and on to the feast of the Baptism of the Lord. Some families keep the tree and crib up through those weeks, and some move the wise men figures closer to the manger each day until the Epiphany.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesse tree: one ornament a night, from the garden to the manger. Your line was the family tree.

On a shelf in a living room, a nativity set. The shepherds are already at the manger, but the wise men aren't. They're on the far side of the room, on top of the bookcase, camels and all. Every morning someone moves them a little closer: across the bookcase, onto the windowsill, along the top of the piano. The rest of the street has dragged its trees to the curb, and these figures are still traveling. They won't reach the manger until the Epiphany. The house is in no hurry, because the feast isn't over.
screen: `THE SHEPHERDS ARE ALREADY THERE.` → `THE WISE MEN ARE ON THE BOOKCASE.` → `STILL TRAVELING.`

segments.voice: First, the count. The twelve days run from Christmas to the Epiphany, the feast of the wise men, which you met in your first year. They come after Christmas, not before it. The shops count down to the day; the Church counts forward from it. And in the Church's calendar the Christmas season runs on past the Epiphany, to the feast of the Baptism of the Lord. Next, the walking wise men. Moving the figures a little each day is a home custom, not a law, but it makes the twelve days visible. Matthew's Gospel says the wise men saw a star and came looking for the newborn king; in some homes they get there one bookshelf at a time. Then, an odd thing: the day after Christmas, the Church keeps the feast of Stephen, a deacon stoned to death in Acts. As the stones fall, the Douay-Rheims says: "And they stoned Stephen, invoking, and saying: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Soon after come the Holy Innocents, the children of Bethlehem killed by Herod. Joy and grief share the same week; the Church doesn't keep grief away from the crib. That's part of keeping the feast: celebrating with your eyes open. Last, the keeping. Paul, calling Christ our Passover, tells the Corinthians to keep the feast with sincerity and truth instead of the old leaven of malice. Keeping a feast is a choice made on ordinary days: lights left on in the window, someone invited over on a weekday, merry Christmas said when everyone else has moved on. Small, stubborn acts of celebration.

1399.title: Easter baskets
1399.hook: Polish Catholics bring food to be blessed on Holy Saturday
1399.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday, Polish Catholic families, in Poland and in Polish parishes elsewhere, bring baskets of Easter food to church to be blessed by a priest or deacon, then share the food at breakfast on Easter morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve days: wise men crossing the living room one shelf at a time. Your line was keep the feast.

Holy Saturday morning, in a Polish parish. The church is strangely quiet; there's no Mass during the day. But the aisle fills anyway, with families carrying wicker baskets lined with white cloth and tucked with sprigs of green. Inside: a few painted eggs, a piece of sausage, a heel of bread, a little salt, a spoonful of horseradish, and often a small lamb made of sugar or butter. The baskets go in rows on long tables. A priest comes down the line with holy water and a prayer, spattering the cloth, the eggs and a few delighted children.
screen: `A QUIET CHURCH ON HOLY SATURDAY.` → `BASKETS LINED WITH WHITE CLOTH.` → `HOLY WATER ON THE EGGS.`

segments.voice: First, the day. The Roman Missal describes Holy Saturday as a day when the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, and there's no Mass until the Easter Vigil after dark. Into that quiet, families bring their food: a small act of hope, setting out the Easter meal before Easter has come. Second, the name. In Polish it's święconka, the blessed food, used for the basket and for the custom. Contents vary by family, and people give them meanings as they pack: eggs for new life, bread for Christ the bread of life, salt for what preserves and gives taste, the lamb for the Lamb of God. Those meanings are tradition, passed on at kitchen tables, not rules. Third, the blessing. The Church has blessings for food at Easter, and a priest or deacon asks God to bless the food and the people who will share it. It's grace before meals, written large: the whole Easter table lifted up before anyone eats. Last, the meal. The basket goes home and waits. On Easter morning, families share its food at breakfast, often starting by passing a blessed egg around the table. In John's Gospel, in a breakfast you met in your first year, the risen Jesus stands on a beach at dawn beside a fire with fish on it, and says to his tired friends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come, and dine." Risen from the tomb, in this story, he makes breakfast.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a table you'll sit at soon: who will be there, and what will be on it. See one dish covered with a white cloth, waiting while you wait too, and notice what it's like to prepare a feast before its reason has arrived. If you pray, ask God to bless that food and the people who'll eat it; if you don't, give thanks for them, one by one.
Easter baskets. Baskets of Easter food, eggs, bread, salt and more, brought to church on Holy Saturday to be blessed and shared at Easter breakfast. In Polish, święconka. Today's word.

1400.title: The Day of the Dead
1400.hook: in Mexico, All Souls is kept with altars, marigolds and photographs
1400.howItsDone: In Mexico and among Mexican families elsewhere, Catholics keep All Saints and All Souls as the Día de Muertos: they build home altars with photographs, candles, marigolds and the favorite foods of those who have died, visit and decorate graves, and pray for the dead, often including Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter baskets: eggs and bread under a white cloth, blessed on Holy Saturday. Your line was święconka.

A table against the living room wall, covered in a bright cloth. On it, a framed photograph of a grandfather in a pressed shirt. Beside him, a glass of water, a candle, a plate of sweet bread, a pack of the cigarettes he never quit, and a bottle of the soda he liked. Marigolds everywhere, petals in a path to the door. A crucifix or Our Lady of Guadalupe watches over it all. Later, the family will clean his grave, bring flowers, and stay a while.
screen: `A PHOTOGRAPH IN A PRESSED SHIRT.` → `MARIGOLDS IN A PATH TO THE DOOR.` → `STAYING A WHILE AT THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the calendar. The Church keeps the Solemnity of All Saints and, the next day, the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, All Souls, which you met in year two, when Catholics pray for everyone who has died. In Mexico, those two days became the Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, kept at home altars and in cemeteries as well as at Mass. Historians discuss how much it also carries older Indigenous ways of honoring the dead. Second, the altar, the ofrenda, which means an offering. Photographs, so faces aren't forgotten. Favorite food and drink, because love remembers details. Candles, for light. Marigolds, whose color and scent, people say, help the dead find their way home. Those meanings are tradition, held with affection. Third, why a Catholic can keep it with joy. The book of Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims: "But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them." Catholics believe the dead are alive in God, and that the living can still pray for them. So it isn't spooky, or a version of Halloween. It's a family reunion across the line of death, with the Church's prayers at its center. Last, this week faith kept leaving the sanctuary: a Mass for someone, a fast, alms in Lent, a Jesse tree, walking wise men, an Easter basket. Today the whole family joins it at home, the living and the dead.
screen: `ALL SAINTS, THEN ALL SOULS.` · `THE OFRENDA: PHOTOS, FOOD, LIGHT.` · `IN THE HAND OF GOD.` · `A WEEK OF FAITH AT HOME.` · then, large: `THE SOULS OF THE JUST ARE IN THE HAND OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Choose one person who has died; if you have a picture nearby, look at their face. Remember one small thing they loved, a food, a song, a joke, a chair they always sat in, and let a smile come if it comes. If you pray, ask God to give them eternal rest; if you don't, say their name and thank them for one thing. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
